A Custom Error Class

ApiError — the deliberate error object Lesson 1's error handler was always ready to read a status from.

Lesson 1's centralized error handler read err.status || 500 from day one (Figure 1.11) — but nothing in this project actually set .status on an error yet, so every thrown error fell through to a generic 500. That slide flagged it directly: "a schema-based version arrives with Zod in Week 3" — this is that arrival, plus the other half of it: a real error object controllers can throw on purpose, with the right status already attached.

// Figure 3.2: an error that knows its own HTTP status (src/utils/ApiError.js)
export default class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, details) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ApiError';
    this.status = status;
    this.details = details;
  }
}

extends Error means an ApiError is a real JavaScript Error — instanceof Error still works, it still has a .message, .stack, and so on — just with two extra properties: status (the HTTP status this error should produce) and an optional details (the field-by-field list a validation failure attaches — previous topic's validate.js). super(message) is required before anything else in a subclass constructor — it's what actually sets up the Error half of this object before the two custom fields are added on top of it.

throw new ApiError(404, 'Ticket 5 not found') anywhere inside an asyncHandler-wrapped controller now reaches the centralized error handler with exactly the status this line chose — no controller needs its own res.status(...).json(...) call to make that happen, which is the whole point of Lesson 1's "no controller handles its own errors" rule holding up under a real, growing CRUD API.
